situations.title: Travel in China
situations.intro: Getting around mainland China: greetings, help, transport, hotels, food, paying and emergencies.

scenes.title: Greetings and politeness basics
scenes.description: What a traveller says all day: hello to one person, to a group and politely; thank you and the replies; sorry vs excuse me (对不起 / 不好意思 / 打扰一下 / 请问); goodbye; short yes/no-type answers; declining an offer; plus the formulas shop and restaurant staff say to you.

phrases.english: Hello! / Hi!
phrases.usage: The all-purpose greeting to one person (HSK level 1). Official listening items use it as a greeting (女：你好！ 男：你好！很高兴认识你。) and, very usefully for travellers, as the polite attention-getter before a request to shop staff, a cashier or a taxi driver: 你好，这个电视多少钱？ / 你好，鱼怎么卖呢？ / 你好，我去世界公园。 / 你好，一共多少钱？ You will hear 你好 or 您好 back. For older people or formal situations use 您好 (see below). With friends, family and people you see every day 你好 sounds stiff — greet them by name or title, with 早 in the morning, or casually (see the rule on greeting people you know).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: Thank you! / Thanks!
phrases.usage: Standard thanks (HSK level 1). Add a pronoun for warmth or respect: 谢谢你 / 谢谢您 (polite) / 谢谢你们 (to several people). The usual reply you will hear is 不客气. The second syllable is neutral tone in the dictionary form (xièxie).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: You're welcome.
phrases.usage: The standard reply to 谢谢 (HSK level 1): 男：谢谢你们！ 女：不客气。再见。 / 男：谢谢！麻烦你们了。 女：不客气。 Dictionary alternatives with the same job: 别客气 'don't mention it; no formalities, please', 不用谢 'You're welcome', 应该的 '(polite response) you're welcome; just doing my duty' (all CC-CEDICT). Pronunciation: 不 is bù in citation form but is said bú before the fourth tone of 客 — that is why the HSK syllabus prints 'bú kèqi'.
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: I'm sorry.
phrases.usage: A real apology when you did something wrong or caused trouble. 现汉: '对人有愧，常用为表示抱歉的套语' (feeling one has wronged someone; the usual formula of apology), e.g. 对不起，让您久等了 'sorry to keep you waiting'. The normal reply is 没关系 (paired exactly so in the HSK 3.0 level-1 sample). Staff also use it when refusing: 先生，对不起，我们这儿不能抽烟。 For small everyday slips 不好意思 is the lighter choice (see rule).
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: That's OK. / It doesn't matter.
phrases.usage: The reply to 对不起 or 不好意思. Also accepts a small problem: 男：好吧，没关系。 (after hearing no window seat is left). 没事 / 没事儿 is also heard in reassurance: 没事，不用担心 'it's nothing, don't worry'.

phrases.english: Sorry. / Excuse me. (for a small inconvenience)
phrases.usage: Light apology for small slips or for troubling someone: 甲：你的词典呢？ 乙：不好意思，我没拿来。 / 不好意思，我忘记拿词典了，下星期一还你行吗？ / 真不好意思，初次见面我就迟到了，让你久等了。 It is also the everyday “excuse me” before a request (不好意思，我迷路了。 “Excuse me, I’m lost.”), and staff use it when they can’t help (不好意思，这里不能地铁直达。 “Sorry, the metro doesn’t go there directly.”). In native-speaker service dialogues it is about four times as frequent as 对不起. CC-CEDICT lists “to be sorry (for inconveniencing sb)” next to “to feel embarrassed” (the 5th-edition 现汉 text available here gives only the “embarrassed / too shy to” senses). HSK 2025: level 2.
phrases.speaker: either

phrases.english: Excuse me. (sorry to bother you)
phrases.usage: Say it to approach a stranger or interrupt someone; in the official examples it is followed by 请问 and the question: 打扰一下，请问，地铁站离这儿远吗？ / 打扰一下，请问在哪儿买票？ The current HSK 3.0 level-4 sample uses it to interrupt students: 打扰一下，同学，请不要在自习室里大声讨论。 When you leave after taking someone's time you can say 打扰了 ('sorry to have bothered you', CC-CEDICT), as in 好的，那我过一会儿再联系吧，打扰了，再见。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Excuse me, what time is it?
phrases.usage: 请问 'may I ask' is the polite opener for any question to a stranger (现汉: 敬辞，用于请求对方回答问题; CC-CEDICT: 'Excuse me, may I ask...?'). Put it right before the question: 请问，这个电视多少钱？ / 请问洗手间在哪儿？ It can follow 你好/您好 or 打扰一下. This exact question is the example item of both the HSK 3.0 level-1 sample paper and the 2025 new-HSK samples.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Hello! (polite)
phrases.usage: Polite hello with the respectful 'you' 您 (现汉: 你/你们 '含敬意', with respect). In official dialogues it is what service staff say to customers (您好，请问您去哪儿？ — taxi driver; 先生，您好，您要办理什么业务？ — bank clerk; 您好！欢迎光临。 — restaurant). Use it yourself with older people, in formal settings, or to be extra polite before a favour: 您好！您能帮我们照张相吗？
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: 您 is routine in Beijing and the north; many southern speakers, whose home dialects have no 你/您 distinction, use it less among themselves (forum reports, anecdotal). 您好 from service staff is normal everywhere, and using 您 to older people — for example a partner’s parents — is polite in any region.

phrases.english: No thanks. (no need)
phrases.usage: Polite refusal of an offer: 女：吃点儿蛋糕吧？很好吃。 男：不用了，谢谢。 Add a reason to soften it: 不用了，我自己打车就行，谢谢你。 (“No need — I’ll just take a taxi, thank you”) / 不用了，谢谢您，我自己能行。 现汉: 不用 = “表示事实上没有必要” (there is no need). It is also the friendly way to wave off a street seller or tout; if someone keeps pushing, the firmer 不要，谢谢 (next phrase) is normal. To a shop assistant who comes over you can say 我只是看看 (“I’m just looking”).
phrases.speaker: me

rules.rule: The level-1 politeness core is 你好 / 谢谢 / 对不起 / 再见, with the replies 不客气 (to thanks) and 没关系 (to an apology). Learners are expected to recognise and exchange these in meeting, parting and everyday situations.
rules.why: The 2025 HSK task syllabus (in force 2026-07) lists exchanging exactly these as a level-1 communicative task; the HSK 3.0 level-1 sample tests the 对不起 → 没关系 and 谢谢 → 不客气 pairs.

rules.rule: 您 is the respectful 'you'. Service staff address customers with 您 / 您好 (您好，请问您去哪儿？ / 您稍等). Use 您 yourself with older people, people you want to show respect to, and in formal situations. In the official dialogues customers address shop staff, clerks and drivers with 你好 + their request (你好，这个电视多少钱？ / 你好，鱼怎么卖呢？ / 你好，我想办一张信用卡。 / 你好，一共多少钱？).
rules.why: 现汉 defines 您 as 你/你们 with respect ('含敬意'); the official HSK dialogues consistently show staff using 您 and customers opening with 你好.
rules.regional_note: Forum reports (anecdotal) say 您 is used routinely in Beijing, even between colleagues, while many southern speakers — whose home dialects, such as Shanghainese, have no 你/您 distinction — use it less in everyday Mandarin. Service staff say 您 everywhere, and 您 to older people (for example a partner’s parents) is polite in any region.

rules.rule: Addressing people you don't know: get staff's attention with 你好 or, in restaurants and hotels, 服务员 (服务员，请给我来一杯咖啡。 / 服务员，我们想再要一个菜。). Call a taxi driver or any skilled worker (a cook 厨师傅, a carpenter 木匠师傅) 师傅 (师傅，我去火车站。); 师傅 also follows a surname (王师傅). Staff will call you 先生 'sir' or 女士 'madam' (both HSK level 1). Students are addressed as 同学 (同学，请问图书馆怎么走？ / 打扰一下，同学，……).
rules.why: 现汉: 师傅 = '对有技艺的人的尊称' (respectful title for someone with a skill/trade), 服务员 = staff who serve guests in hotels, restaurants etc.; CC-CEDICT adds 'respectful form of address for older men' for 师傅. The forms are shown in use in official HSK/YCT dialogues.

rules.rule: In mainland China do not call a waitress or shop assistant 小姐 on its own: the word picked up the slang sense “sex worker”, and the older textbooks that taught it are out of date. Use 服务员 or 你好 instead (美女 / 帅哥 in casual places — see the next rule). Surname + 小姐 (王小姐 “Ms Wang”) is still fine in formal and business settings, and 女士 is the safe formal “madam”. In Taiwan and Hong Kong 小姐 for staff is still normal.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT records the slang sense “(slang) prostitute” for 小姐. The 2009-2010 Hanban HSK papers still had customers call female staff 小姐 (小姐，请问表演什么时候开始？ / 小姐，你好，你这儿有杯子吗？); the national 2021 standard listed 小姐 at level 1, but the 2025 HSK syllabus moved it to level 5, and none of the HSK 3.0 / 2025 sample items examined uses it as a call to staff. Current teaching sources (Kaiwa 2026, italki, Digmandarin, Chinese-forums) agree that bare 小姐 is avoided for staff in the mainland while 王小姐-style name + 小姐 remains usable.
rules.regional_note: Teaching sources say the negative connotation is felt most strongly in northern cities such as Beijing and Harbin and less in the south — but avoiding bare 小姐 for staff is the safe choice everywhere in the mainland.

rules.rule: 美女 (“beautiful woman”) and 帅哥 (“handsome guy”) are widely used as casual forms of address, especially to call young staff in shops and restaurants. They are informal, and some people find them a bit tacky (土) or uncomfortable, so with older people or in formal places stick to 你好, 服务员, 师傅 and 先生 / 女士.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT lists “handsome (form of address)” under 帅哥; the dictionaries do not record the address use of 美女, but magazine and teaching sources do: The World of Chinese (2018) says both are still used in the service industry (popular from the mid-2000s to the early 2010s, with a somewhat working-class flavour); Digmandarin calls them relaxed address terms between peers; a Kunming forum thread reports 美女 / 帅哥 as the local way to call waiting staff, with some finding it “uncouth” and younger educated speakers preferring 服务员; a 2026 teaching blog recommends 美女 for staff only in casual places.

rules.rule: Choose the “sorry / excuse me” word by situation: 对不起 = apology when you have wronged or troubled someone (reply 没关系); 不好意思 = lighter “sorry” for small slips and inconveniences, and the everyday “excuse me” before a request; 抱歉 = “sorry”, used e.g. by staff and in announcements (抱歉，先生，这里禁止吸烟。 / 我们很抱歉地通知您……); 打扰一下 = “excuse me” when approaching or interrupting someone; 请问 = “may I ask”, placed directly before a question. Sequence attested for approaching strangers: 打扰一下，请问，… ？ In Beijing you may also hear 劳驾 (“excuse me / may I trouble you”, also to get past people); it is northern and rather old-fashioned, so use 请问, 不好意思 or 打扰一下 yourself — especially in the south.
rules.why: 现汉 defines 对不起 as the apology formula for having wronged someone and 请问 as an honorific for asking someone to answer a question; CC-CEDICT gives 不好意思 “to be sorry (for inconveniencing sb)” and 打扰了 “sorry to interrupt you”; the official dialogues show each word in these roles. On 劳驾: teaching and dictionary sites (HanyuGuide, FluentU, That’s Mandarin) describe it as northern and old-fashioned, the 2025 HSK syllabus places it at levels 7-9, and native-speaker dialogue corpora use 请问 about 700 times as often.

rules.rule: Spoken morning greeting: 早 or 早上好. 早安 also means “good morning”, but in the mainland it is mostly written (good-morning messages on WeChat and social media) and more usual in Taiwan; said aloud it can sound a little formal or literary. 晚安 means “good night” when parting, not “good evening” as a greeting (that is 晚上好).
rules.why: 现汉 entries 早 (sense ❺), 早安 (“多见于翻译作品” in the 5th-edition text) and 晚安 (“用于晚上道别”); CC-CEDICT 晚上好 “Good evening!”; the 新华 词语 data defines 早安 as a greeting formula (“套语。用于早晨见面时互相问候”); teaching sites (Migaku, Preply) describe 早上好 as the mainland standard and 早安 as typical of Taiwan and written messages.

rules.rule: 你好 is for strangers, service staff and first meetings. With friends, family and people you see every day it sounds stiff and formal. Greet them instead by name or title (老师好 to a teacher), with 早 in the morning, with a casual 嗨 / 哈喽 (common among younger people), with a small question about their day (吃了吗？ “have you eaten?”, 去哪儿？ “where are you off to?”), or with 好久不见 when you haven’t met for a while.
rules.why: Teaching sites (LTL, Hack Chinese, New Concept Mandarin, an Everyday Chinese course) describe 你好 as formal, used mainly when meeting someone new and not normally among friends, and list these alternatives; native-speaker dialogue writers open casually with 哈喽 / 嗨 as well as 你好.

scenes.title: When you don't understand
scenes.description: Signalling that you didn't hear or didn't understand, asking for a repeat, checking meaning and pronunciation, saying how much Chinese you speak, asking for English, and asking someone to wait.

phrases.english: I didn't understand (what you said).
phrases.usage: Say it when you heard the words but didn't understand them: 男：天“短”了是什么意思？我没听懂。 / 女：对不起，我没听懂，您说得太快了。 没听懂 = didn't catch/understand this time. For a general inability (e.g. a strong accent or dialect) the dictionary form is 听不懂 'unable to make sense of what one is hearing' (CC-CEDICT), as in the national standard's example 刚来中国时，他一句中文也听不懂。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.literal: sorry, I not hear-understand, you(respectful) speak (complement) too fast (particle)
phrases.english: Sorry, I didn't understand — you spoke too fast.
phrases.usage: The polite way, attested verbatim, to signal that you need it slower. A variant for someone reading aloud: 对不起，您读得太快，我没听懂。 The direct request is 请说慢一点 (see that phrase).

phrases.pinyin: Nǐ shuō shénme? Wǒ méi tīngjiàn.
phrases.literal: you say what? I not hear-perceive
phrases.english: What did you say? I didn't hear (you).
phrases.usage: For when you literally didn’t hear (noise, a bad phone line). 没听见 = didn’t hear; 没听懂 = heard but didn’t understand. On the phone: 女：喂？你听见我说话了吗？ 男：你说什么？你再说一次？ With a stranger a softer opener is 不好意思，我没听清楚 (“sorry, I didn’t catch that”) — 现汉’s example: 你刚才说的话我没听清楚，你从起头儿再说一遍。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.usage: Casual “say it again” to someone you know: in the source a woman who lost her phone asks a friend for his number again (以前有，我的电话丢了，再说一次吧。); on a bad line: 你说什么？你再说一次？ To a stranger use 请再说一遍 or 不好意思，能再说一遍吗？ (see those phrases) — 再说一遍 (遍 = one complete run-through, 现汉) is also the more common wording in native-speaker dialogues.

phrases.usage: SLOT CHANGED: the source sentence is 你会说汉语吗？ ('Do you speak Chinese?'); only the language name was replaced (汉语 → 英语). 英文 is also used for 'English' (CC-CEDICT gives both 英语 and 英文 as 'English (language)'; national standard example: 除了英文，他还会说中文。). phrases.english: I've only learned a little Chinese.
phrases.usage: Shortened from the national standard's example 在来中国以前，我只学过一点儿中文。 ('Before coming to China I had only studied a little Chinese'): the time phrase 在来中国以前 was dropped (time slot); keep it if it fits. Tells people you can try in Chinese but need simple language. 中文 and 汉语 both mean the Chinese language (both HSK level 1).
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: 一点儿 with the -r ending is northern (Beijing) speech; speakers from the south usually say 一点 (yīdiǎn): 我只学过一点中文。

rules.rule: Pick the verb for what went wrong: 没听见 = I didn’t hear it; 没听懂 = I heard it but didn’t understand; 听不懂 = I can’t understand (the speech/language — also a dialect: 我听不懂粤语 “I can’t understand Cantonese”); 看不懂 = I can’t make sense of something written or seen (sign, map, menu); 不明白 = I don’t understand the meaning or the point.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 听见 'to hear', 听懂 'to understand (on hearing)', 听不懂 'unable to make sense of what one is hearing', 看不懂 'unable to make sense of what one is looking at'; 现汉 明白 ❹ '知道；了解'. Official items use them exactly so (你说什么？我没听见。 / 我没听懂 / 这张地图我看不懂 / 有个句子的意思我不明白).

scenes.title: Asking for help and directions
scenes.description: Asking where something is and how to get there, whether it is far, finding the toilet or a metro station, saying you are lost, asking a stranger for a favour — and the typical answers you will hear (go straight, turn left/right, opposite, right ahead, not far).

phrases.english: Excuse me, where is the toilet?
phrases.usage: Pattern 请问 + place + 在哪儿？ Official exchange: 男：请问洗手间在哪儿？ 女：您向前走，左边就是。 Also attested with 哪里: 请问，男洗手间在哪里？ ('Where is the men's toilet?'). 洗手间 is the polite word (现汉: 婉辞，指厕所). Swap the place (slot): 地铁站 metro station, 出口 exit, 二零四房间 room 204 (请问，二零四房间在哪儿？).
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Speakers from the south usually say 哪里 (请问洗手间在哪里？); 哪儿 with the -r ending is typical of Beijing and the north. Both are standard and understood everywhere.

phrases.hanzi: 您好！您能帮我们照张相吗？
phrases.pinyin: Nín hǎo! Nín néng bāng wǒmen zhào zhāng xiàng ma?
phrases.literal: you(respectful)-good! you(respectful) can help us take (measure) photo (question)
phrases.english: Hello! Could you take a photo of us?
phrases.usage: 能…吗 'could you…' with 帮 'help (do sth for)' is the basic polite request frame. The official dialogue continues: 男：当然可以。 … 男：没问题。准备好了吗？笑一笑，一，二，三。 ('No problem. Ready? Smile — one, two, three'). Children's version in YCT: 阿姨，能帮我们照张相吗？ A generic 'Can you help me?' sentence was not found in the sources seen (see open_questions).
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.hanzi: 你再向南走两百米就能看到了。
phrases.pinyin: Nǐ zài xiàng nán zǒu liǎngbǎi mǐ jiù néng kàndào le.
phrases.literal: you further toward south walk two-hundred metre then can see (particle)
phrases.english: Walk another 200 metres south and you'll see it.
phrases.usage: Directions may use compass points (东 east, 南 south, 西 west, 北 north) instead of left/right. Other official answers: 就在路东 ('on the east side of the road'), 就在超市西边 ('just west of the supermarket'), 北门左边 ('left of the north gate'). Here the asker had said 我现在就在学校西门 ('I'm at the school's west gate').
phrases.speaker: them
phrases.regional_note: Teaching sources say compass directions are typical of northern cities with grid-plan streets (e.g. Beijing), while in southern cities, with rivers and hills, people more often say left/right (and up/down). This is a widely repeated impression rather than a studied rule — in the south be ready for both.

rules.rule: Asking the way: [打扰一下，] 请问 + place + 在哪儿？ / 去 + place + 怎么走？ / 附近有 + place + 吗？ / place + 离这儿远吗？ Thank with 谢谢 or 好的，谢谢. Asking the way and understanding simple directions (direction, position, route, time) is an HSK level-1/level-2 task.
rules.why: All four question frames occur in official HSK/YCT dialogues; the 2025 HSK task syllabus lists 问路 (asking the way) and understanding 指路 (directions: 行进方向、位置、路线、时长、乘车信息) at levels 1-2.

rules.rule: Be ready for compass points in directions: 东 (east), 南 (south), 西 (west), 北 (north) — e.g. 向南走两百米, 就在路东, 就在超市西边, 北门左边.
rules.why: Several official answers give directions this way instead of (or together with) left/right.
rules.regional_note: Teaching sources say compass directions are typical of northern cities with grid-plan streets (e.g. Beijing), while in southern cities people more often use left/right (and up/down). This is a widely repeated impression rather than a studied rule — be ready for both.

rules.rule: Three words for 'toilet': 洗手间 = the polite euphemism (the polite choice when asking); 卫生间 = a room with sanitary fittings, i.e. the bathroom/toilet of a flat or hotel, also a toilet in general; 厕所 = the general, non-euphemistic word. HSK 2025 levels: 洗手间 2, 卫生间 3, 厕所 4.

rules.rule: 哪儿 and 哪里 both mean 'where' and are both HSK level-1 words; 现汉 labels 哪儿 as colloquial (〈口〉) and defines it as 哪里. Official dialogues use both for the same question (请问洗手间在哪儿？ / 请问，男洗手间在哪里？). The same pairing exists for 这儿/这里 'here' and 那儿/那里 'there'.
rules.why: 2025 HSK vocabulary syllabus (哪里 nǎlǐ, 哪儿 nǎr, level 1); 现汉 entries 哪儿 and 那儿 (〈口〉).
rules.regional_note: The -r (儿化) forms 哪儿 / 这儿 / 那儿 / 一点儿 are typical of Beijing and northern speech; southern speakers usually avoid them and say 哪里, 这里, 那里 and 一点 (some Southwestern Mandarin areas such as Chengdu and Chongqing do use -r). From a south/central-China family you are likely to hear 哪里 / 这里 / 一点 more often; both sets are standard. In native-speaker dialogue corpora 哪里 outnumbers 哪儿 about 8 to 1, and 这里 outnumbers 这儿 about 9 to 1.

situations.title: Family
situations.intro: Meeting and visiting your partner's family: forms of address, gifts, dinner, small talk and festivals.

scenes.title: Meeting your partner's parents: what to call them and what to say
scenes.description: How to address your partner's parents before marriage (叔叔/阿姨, or 伯父/伯母) and after the wedding (改口 to 爸/妈, usually at the wedding tea ceremony, with the 改口费 gift), short polite lines for a first visit, and what the hosts will say to you. Evidence: CC-CEDICT, the 现代汉语词典 transcription, official HSK/YCT papers and syllabi, Tatoeba sentences, Xinhua data, relationship.js, and (for current etiquette) a few web articles read through search-result summaries.

phrases.english: Uncle — what you call your partner's father (or any man of your parents' generation) before you are married
phrases.usage: Before marriage a friend's or partner's parents are 叔叔 and 阿姨: in the official HSK 3 sample paper a man about to marry tells a friend '让叔叔、阿姨也一起来' (bring your parents — lit. uncle and auntie — along too). CC-CEDICT: 'form of address used by children for a male one generation older'; Xinhua: '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子' (general term for men of one's father's generation who are younger [than one's father]); for a man clearly older than your own father the matching title is 伯父/伯伯. Pair it with 您: HSK 3 sample '叔叔，您愿意教我吗？'. Children will in turn call you 叔叔 if you are a man of their parents' generation. Whether your partner's family expects 叔叔 or 伯父 is not settled by these sources: ask your partner.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Auntie — what you call your partner's mother (or any woman of your parents' generation) before you are married
phrases.usage: The counterpart of 叔叔 (HSK 3 sample: '让叔叔、阿姨也一起来'). Xinhua: '称呼跟母亲辈分相同、年纪差不多的妇女：王～' (address for a woman of one's mother's generation and similar age, e.g. 王阿姨); CC-CEDICT: 'woman of similar age to one's parents (term of address used by child)'. HSK 5 sample: '阿姨，您现在还每天看书吗？' (a young man to a retired woman, with 您). 阿姨 is also how nannies and childcare workers are addressed (Xinhua sense ③; CC-CEDICT 'childcare worker; nursemaid'). Alternative pair: 伯父/伯母.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: Xinhua marks only the kinship sense 'mother's sister' as dialectal (〈方〉); the title sense (王阿姨) has no regional label.

phrases.english: Sorry to bother you. / Sorry for the trouble.
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'sorry to interrupt you, but ... / sorry to have bothered you / sorry, I have to go'. In the HSK 4 sample a visitor who did not find the person ends with '好的，那我过一会儿再联系吧，打扰了，再见。'. So it fits when you interrupt someone and when you take your leave after imposing on them. CC-CEDICT also lists a slang sense (coined c. 2017, mostly online): said facetiously to end a conversation with someone insufferable — your tone makes the difference.

phrases.english: Uncle (respectful) — title for a man of your father's generation who is older than your own father
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'father's elder brother; term of respect for older man'. As a title it strictly suits a man older than your own father (Xinhua defines 叔叔 as the term for the younger ones). HSK 2025 lists 伯父/伯伯/伯母 at level 7-9 and 叔叔/阿姨 at level 3. Whether your partner's family prefers 伯父/伯母 or 叔叔/阿姨 at a first visit is not settled by these sources: ask your partner.
phrases.speaker: me
phrases.regional_note: As a title for a partner's father, 伯父 is understood everywhere. Don't carry over the northern kinship word 大爷 (= your own father's older brother in the north; see the paternal chart): said to an unrelated man, 大爷 is a title for an old man (现代汉语词典 大爷 ❷ '尊称年长的男子').

phrases.english: Mum — how you address your partner's mother once you are married
phrases.usage: After the wedding you 改口 (change how you address them): CC-CEDICT 改口 '…as when one marries and starts to call one's husband's parents 爸爸 and 妈妈'; 改口费 is given to the new daughter-in-law or son-in-law, so the switch concerns both. 妈 is the everyday short form; with 您 it stays respectful, as in the HSK 4 sample '妈，您的手机响了。'. Before the 改口, use 阿姨 (or 伯母). The switch usually happens at the wedding, during the tea ceremony (敬茶, also called 改口茶) when the parents hand over the 改口费; some families invite you to say 妈 earlier (for example once you are engaged or have registered the marriage) — wait for them to offer, and follow your partner's lead.

phrases.english: 'change-of-address money': a cash gift from the parents to their new son- or daughter-in-law at the wedding
phrases.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'a gift of money given by parents on both sides after a wedding, to their new daughter-in-law or son-in-law'. As the name says (改口 + 费 'fee'), it goes with 改口: the parents hand it over when you first call them 爸/妈, typically after you serve them tea at the wedding (改口茶). There is no fixed amount; the two families agree on it, often choosing a lucky number.
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: Who gives it varies: in many places it is the groom's parents giving it to the bride, while in some places (reportedly especially North China) the bride's parents also give it to the groom. Ask your partner what their family and region expect.

rules.rule: Speak to your partner's parents (and other elders) with 您, the courteous 'you', and put their title first: 叔叔，您…; 阿姨，您好. After marriage 您 stays respectful (妈，您…), but follow your partner's lead: many families, especially in the south, say 你 to their own parents.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 您 = 'you (courteous, as opposed to informal 你)'. The official HSK samples show younger speakers pairing titles with 您: '叔叔，您愿意教我吗？', '阿姨，您现在还每天看书吗？', '妈，您的手机响了。', '爸，您为什么要问我这么简单的问题？'. (Some samples show children using 你 with their own parents, e.g. the answer option '爸爸，你累了吧'; for an in-law, 您 is the courteous form.)
rules.regional_note: 您 is far more frequent in northern speech (Beijing above all); in the south many people say 你 even to elders in everyday talk, so 您 can sound a little formal there — but it is never wrong at a first meeting (anecdotal evidence: learner-forum reports).

rules.rule: Before marriage — and especially before you are engaged — call your partner's parents by kinship titles, as you would a friend's parents: 叔叔 (father) and 阿姨 (mother), greeting them with 叔叔阿姨好; or 伯父/伯母 if they are older than your own parents. Surname + title (王阿姨, 张叔叔) is the standard pattern for other older acquaintances, such as neighbours and family friends.
rules.why: HSK 3 sample: a man invites a friend's parents to his wedding as '叔叔、阿姨'. Xinhua: 阿姨 = '称呼跟母亲辈分相同、年纪差不多的妇女'; 叔叔 = '泛称与父同辈而年龄较小的男子'. CC-CEDICT: 伯父 'term of respect for older man', 伯母 'polite form of address for a woman who is about the age of one's mother'. HSK 2025 syllabus: '姓氏+亲属称谓（张爷爷）'.

rules.rule: 改口: you switch to 爸/妈 (爸爸/妈妈) for your partner's parents at the wedding, usually during the tea ceremony (敬茶, also called 改口茶), and they give you 改口费. Before that use 叔叔/阿姨 (or 伯父/伯母), and don't start saying 爸/妈 on your own initiative: some parents invite it earlier (after the engagement or the marriage registration), and then you follow their lead.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT 改口: '…to change the way one addresses sb (as when one marries and starts to call one's husband's parents 爸爸 and 妈妈)'; 改口费: 'a gift of money given by parents on both sides after a wedding, to their new daughter-in-law or son-in-law'. 现代汉语词典/Xinhua 改口 ②: '改变称呼'. Web articles (search summaries): '敬茶又叫"改口茶"…当双方父母喝下新人们敬的茶后，还会给新人们改口费'; '若是两人还没有开始谈婚论嫁…就喊叔叔阿姨是最好的' (maigoo); parents who accept you may say you can call them 爸/媽 (Marie Claire Taiwan); following one's spouse in calling the in-laws 爸爸/媽媽 is still widespread (ETtoday, 2026).
rules.regional_note: Who gives 改口费, and how much, varies by region and family — in some places (reportedly especially North China) the bride's parents also give it to the groom. Ask your partner.

situations.title: Work
situations.intro: Working with Chinese colleagues and clients: titles, introductions, WeChat, meetings and writing.

scenes.title: Titles and forms of address
scenes.description: How to address superiors, colleagues, clients and groups at work: surname + title (王总, 李经理, 王主任, 王工), 老师 as a general courtesy title, surname + 先生/女士, 您 vs 你, familiar 老X/小X and 王姐/李哥, addressing a group (各位, 各位领导、各位同事, 诸位, 您二位), and what not to say (小X to a senior, bare 小姐, 您们 in speech).

phrases.english: you (polite form)
phrases.usage: The respectful 'you'. 现代汉语词典 glosses 您 as 你；你们（含敬意） and calls it the 尊称 (respectful form) of 你; CC-CEDICT: 'you (courteous, as opposed to informal 你)'. In the official workplace dialogues it is used upward and to clients: staff to a general manager 李总，请您在这份文件上签字 (BCT A); a new employee to the boss 谢谢您！谢谢您给我这个机会 (HSK 3); a host to a visiting manager 您好，王经理 (HSK 5). The superior answers with 你 (欢迎你来公司工作) and peers use 你. Use 您 with superiors, clients, older people and at first meetings. 您 takes no -们 (see rule on 您们). When 您 starts to sound too distant with a colleague was not verified in this session.
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: Anecdotal only (learner forum, not a study): 您 is said to be used more, and kept up longer into a relationship, in Beijing and the north, while in the south it is heard less in everyday speech than on TV. Using 您 to superiors, clients and older relatives is respectful standard Mandarin everywhere.

phrases.english: Teacher Zhang (Mr./Ms. Zhang)
phrases.usage: Surname + 老师. The 2025 HSK syllabus gives 姓氏+职业（张老师） as its model of a Chinese form of address, and 现代汉语词典 defines 老师 as 对教师的尊称，泛指传授文化、技术的人或在某方面值得学习的人. Today it is also widely used at work as a general courtesy title for colleagues and contacts, especially when you don't know their title, and especially in media, advertising and internet companies, cultural work and some government offices: newspapers call it a 'catch-all' (万金油) form that fits almost any profession and is neutral about rank and gender, and an etiquette article advises newcomers 不知道怎么叫，就先叫'老师'. Some people find the overuse odd (e.g. calling barbers or clients 老师), and sales-oriented companies tend to use 王姐/李哥-type forms instead, so follow what your colleagues say. Phone example: 喂，是王老师吗？ (GF 0025-2021).
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: A 凤凰网 article notes that in Jinan (济南) and Chongqing (重庆) speech 老师 is itself a broad term of respect for people in general (search-result summary).

phrases.english: (young) Zhang: familiar form for a younger or junior colleague
phrases.usage: 小 + surname is an affectionate, familiar form (新华字典/汉典 data: 小 用在姓、名、排行等之前，表示爱称). In the official workplace texts it is said by a manager or colleague to a junior: 小张，你这份计划书写得不错，就按照这个计划去做市场调查吧 (HSK 4, a manager to an employee); 小林，这次的招聘是由你负责吧？ (HSK 4); a note from 王东: 小张，我去三楼会议室开会了 (Hanban BCT A sample of c. 2013). You may hear it used for you if you are junior. Not a title: do not use it for superiors, clients or older people (see rule): in a 2017 China Youth Daily survey a respondent notes that 小刘-type address is inappropriate when the other person is a senior colleague, and the official texts only use it downward.
phrases.speaker: either
phrases.regional_note: 现代汉语词典 lists 阿 + name/surname (～唐) as a dialectal (〈方〉) familiar form, and CC-CEDICT describes 阿 as a prefix before monosyllabic names to indicate familiarity; which regions use it, and whether at work, was not verified in this session.

phrases.english: Sister Wang: friendly address for a woman colleague a bit older than you (李哥 for a man)
phrases.usage: Surname + 姐 (for a woman) or surname + 哥 (for a man, e.g. 李哥) is a warm, respectful way to address a colleague somewhat older or more senior than you. 现代汉语词典: 姐 ❸ 称呼年轻的女子; 哥 ❸ 称呼年纪跟自己差不多的男子（含亲热意）; 大姐 ❷ 对年纪跟自己相仿的女子的尊称：刘～｜王～. In a 2017 China Youth Daily survey of 1,972 working people, 某哥某姐 was one of the three most common ways newcomers addressed senior colleagues (41.3%, after job titles 46.0% and 师傅 44.2%). It is friendly rather than formal: media reports say it is especially common in sales-oriented companies, while some office and civil-service staff find 哥/姐 too informal for work and use 老师 or job titles. Copy what your colleagues use; as it is informal, it is not the safe choice for clients or senior managers.

rules.rule: At work, address people as surname + job title or profession (王总, 李经理, 王主任, 王工, 王律师, 张老师), or surname + 先生/女士 when no title is used; keep the same form when referring to them (王总希望…). When you are new, listen to how colleagues address each other and copy them; if unsure between two titles, choose the higher one (就高不就低); 老师 is a common neutral fallback when you don't know someone's title. Being able to use Chinese forms of address correctly is listed as a basic workplace communication skill.
rules.why: The 2025 HSK syllabus teaches 姓氏+职业（张老师） as the standard pattern for 称谓语; the official business tests (BCT) and HSK dialogues use it throughout; the vocational Chinese standard T/ISCLT 002-2023 lists correct use of 称谓语 as an entry-level workplace strategy. A 2017 China Youth Daily survey of 1,972 working people (reported by 中国新闻网) found job titles the most common way to address senior colleagues (46.0%), followed by 师傅 (44.2%) and 某哥某姐 (41.3%), and recorded the advice 就高不就低 and 察言观色.

sources.publisher: 中国新闻网, reporting a 中国青年报社会调查中心 survey of 1,972 working people

rules.rule: Use 您 to superiors, clients, older people and people you meet in a formal setting. In the official dialogues superiors answer with 你, and colleagues of the same level use 你 with each other.
rules.why: 现代汉语词典 calls 您 the 尊称 of 你. Official dialogues show the asymmetry: boss → new employee 欢迎你来公司工作, employee → boss 谢谢您！谢谢您给我这个机会 (HSK 3); staff → general manager 李总，请您在这份文件上签字 (BCT A); manager → junior 小林，这次的招聘是由你负责吧？ (HSK 4); employee → boss on the phone 我马上让她联系您 (HSK 5).
rules.regional_note: Anecdotal only (learner forum, not a study): 您 is said to be used more, and kept up longer, in Beijing and the north, while in everyday southern speech it is heard less than on TV. Using 您 to superiors, clients and older relatives is respectful standard Mandarin everywhere.

rules.rule: Avoid 您们 in speech. To two people say 您二位 or 您俩 (您三位 for three); to a group say 各位 or 大家; plain 你们 is normal and polite enough (a guest thanks the hosts with 谢谢你们的热情招待). You will still see 您们 in service messages and letters: native writers do use it, but the dictionaries and teaching standards do not list it, so many teachers mark it as non-standard.
rules.why: Dictionary note (新华字典/汉典 data): 您 用于多数时不加词尾“们”; 现代汉语词典 glosses 您 itself as 你；你们（含敬意） (example 您二位想吃点儿什么？) and has no entry 您们; the GF 0025-2021 list of personal pronouns (我、你、您、他、她、我们、你们、他们、她们) has no 您们. Usage: OpenSubtitles 2018 zh_cn counts 您们 136 vs 你们 207,368; the jieba lexicon lists 您们 20 vs 你们 21,386; in the human-to-human RiSAWOZ/CrossWOZ service dialogues the agents write 您们 12 times and 你们 868 times; and when a learner wrote 您们 in a thank-you letter, 7 of 13 native corrections in the YACLC corpus kept it and 5 changed it to 你们. Native speakers are divided, so 你们/各位/您二位 is the safe choice.

rules.rule: 老 + surname (老王) and 小 + surname (小张) are familiar forms, not titles. 老 marks familiarity; 小 is an affectionate form, and in the official workplace texts 小X is always said by a manager or colleague to a junior or younger person (小张，你这份计划书写得不错…; 小林，这次的招聘是由你负责吧？), while colleagues call each other 老王.
rules.why: Dictionary senses: 老 前缀，用于称人 (现代汉语词典), 'to indicate affection or familiarity' (CC-CEDICT); 小 用在姓、名、排行等之前，表示爱称 (新华字典/汉典 data). Usage pattern from the official HSK 4 and BCT samples.

rules.rule: Do not call a superior, a client or a senior colleague 小X; use their title (王总, 李经理, 王主任…) with 您, or the 老师 / 王姐-type form your colleagues use. 老X is for peers you know well; using it for your boss or a client would be over-familiar unless they invite it.
rules.why: A 2017 China Youth Daily (中国青年报) survey of 1,972 working people, reported by 中国新闻网, quotes a respondent: calling someone 小刘 is not appropriate if that person is a senior colleague (前辈). 新华字典 defines 小 before a surname as an affectionate form (表示爱称), and every official sample uses 小X downward (小张，你这份计划书写得不错…; 小林，这次的招聘是由你负责吧？). The 老X advice is an inference from the dictionary sense (familiarity) and the official samples, where 老王 is used between peers; no source states it.

rules.rule: To address a woman formally, use surname + 女士 or her job title. Be careful with 小姐: it is also slang for women in the sex trade (CC-CEDICT: '(slang) prostitute'; an academic article of 2005 already describes the clash between the old and new meanings), so as a bare form of address (小姐！) it has become awkward on the mainland and many women dislike it. In service settings people now often say 美女 instead, which is informal and which some find flippant, so not for work. Older official material still uses 小姐 neutrally (HSK 5 sample: 小姐，你好，我是来应聘的; 是王小姐让我下午两点半来面试的), so you will meet it in textbooks; whether surname + 小姐 is still usual in mainland offices was not specifically checked.
rules.why: 现代汉语词典: 女士 对妇女的尊称; 小姐 (5th-edition text) 对年轻的女子或未出嫁的女子的称呼; CC-CEDICT 小姐: young lady; miss; (slang) prostitute. 河海大学学报 (2005): 由于'小姐'被用来指称三陪女、发廊按摩女，传统用法与新用法产生冲突，给交际带来尴尬; Language Log: 小姐, 姑娘, 美女 and 女士 are still used but less commonly than before.

phrases.literal: everyone good, I am-called Zhang Ming, am Peking University 's student
phrases.english: Hello everyone, I'm Zhang Ming, a student at Peking University.
phrases.usage: Model self-introduction to a group (CLEC YCT 4 sample): 你先做个自我介绍吧。 — 大家好，我叫张明，是北京大学的学生。 Frame: 大家好 + 我叫 [name] + 是 [organisation] 的 [role]. At work, fill the slots with your company and role (a slot change; the exact work version 我是X公司的Y was not seen in a source in this session). Related official form: 我姓李，是各位的导游。 (HSK 4). A first-day self-introduction at a meeting is a task in the official BCT speaking sample (你今天入职，和同事一起开会，你会怎样介绍自己？). For a work meeting, open with 各位领导、各位同事，大家好！ and close with 请大家多多关照。 (see those items).

rules.rule: Shaking hands at work: stand up (rise if you are seated), lean slightly forward, offer your right hand at about one metre, smile and look at the person; shake for 2-3 seconds, moving 2-3 times, palm to palm, with a moderate grip. The superior offers his or her hand first to a subordinate; between a man and a woman the woman offers first (if she does not, the man nods); with several people go by status or age, or simply from nearest to farthest.

rules.rule: 幸会, 久仰 and 指教 are fixed courtesies (客套话) for first meetings and formal settings. In business they are often doubled (幸会幸会, 久仰久仰) or extended (久仰大名). 幸会 counts as core business vocabulary (BCT A list); 久仰 is advanced (HSK 7-9) and rarer; some native speakers find these stiff, and the plain greetings of the official samples (很高兴认识你, HSK 1; 您好，很高兴见到您, BCT A) do the same job.
rules.why: 现代汉语词典 labels 久仰 (初次见面时说), 幸会 and 指教 ❷ as 客套话; 幸会 is on the BCT (A) 600-word list; 久仰 is HSK 7-9 in the 2025 syllabus; subtitle counts: 幸会 1,676, 久仰 137. 新华 data example: 久仰大名，今日幸会了; teaching sources (search-result summaries): 幸会 is usually said twice in business, 久仰 is for professionals meeting for the first time rather than friends; a native speaker on a learner forum prefers 很高兴认识你 to the 'cold' 幸会.

rules.rule: 面子 ('face') is a person's public standing and self-esteem. People avoid situations where they could 丢面子 (lose face), and favours are sometimes granted 看在X的面子上 ('out of regard for X'). Practical consequence (inference, not stated as a rule in the sources seen): avoid embarrassing someone in front of others, e.g. correcting a superior or client publicly.

dialogues.title: Exchanging names with a new business contact

scenes.title: Exchanging contacts
scenes.description: Giving your business card, asking for and leaving phone numbers, adding each other on WeChat (加个微信吧, 我扫你还是你扫我), WeChat and business-card etiquette, business email formulas, phone calls (asking for someone, holding, messages) and the QR-code wording you will read.

phrases.hanzi: 您好，很高兴见到您，这是我的名片。
phrases.pinyin: Nín hǎo, hěn gāoxìng jiàndào nín, zhè shì wǒ de míngpiàn.
phrases.literal: hello(polite), very glad see you(polite), this is my name-card
phrases.english: Hello, very nice to meet you. Here is my business card.
phrases.usage: Handing over your business card at a first meeting (official BCT (A) sample: the writing item gives the pinyin míngpiàn for the gap). 名片 = 交际时所用的向人介绍自己的长方形硬纸片，上面印着自己的姓名、职务、地址等 (现代汉语词典); BCT (A) core word. For how to hand over and receive cards see the business-card rule; a common humble variant is 这是我的名片，请多指教。
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.hanzi: 把手机号留下吧，以便跟你联系。
phrases.pinyin: Bǎ shǒujīhào liúxià ba, yǐbiàn gēn nǐ liánxì.
phrases.literal: (object marker) mobile-number leave (suggestion), so-that with you contact
phrases.english: Leave me your mobile number so we can stay in touch.
phrases.usage: Asking for a mobile number (GF 0025-2021 grammar example for 以便). 以便 ('so that') is a somewhat formal connective (现代汉语词典's example is a written notice); in conversation 方便 + 联系 is a lighter alternative, as in the HSK 4 sample 请您留个电话号码，方便师傅与您联系. 手机号 (mobile number) is not a CC-CEDICT headword; it is 手机 + 号 and is used in the official standards and tests (小王的手机号是多少？). With superiors or clients use 您 instead of 你 (slot change).
phrases.speaker: me

rules.rule: Business phone calls: avoid calling before 7:00, after 22:00, at dinner time, or at midday if the person naps; keep calls short (about 3-5 minutes) and prepare your points. Open with 您好, use 请 often, close with 谢谢. Answer before the third ring or apologise (对不起，让您久等了). When answering, introduce yourself first, then politely ask who is calling; if the person asked for is absent, offer to take a message. Do not eat, drink or talk to others during the call.
rules.why: Reading passage on business phone etiquette in the Hanban BCT (B) sample paper (c. 2013, early WeChat era; still the only phone-etiquette source seen in this session).

rules.rule: Business cards: hand over and receive cards with both hands (the safe choice in mainland China), then take a moment to read the card (name, title, company) before putting it in a card holder or on the table next to you. Don't stuff it into a trouser or back pocket, and don't write on someone's card in front of them. In tech and start-up circles, scanning WeChat QR codes has largely replaced paper cards.
rules.why: Etiquette guides for China (LC Chinese School '10 Tips', Juwai, HSK Lord) and a Taiwanese job-site etiquette article (104 人力銀行) agree on both hands, reading the card first and not pocketing it at once; LC Chinese School says not to write on a card until the person is out of sight; HSK Lord notes that WeChat QR codes have largely replaced paper cards in tech and start-up circles. (Search-result summaries; the pages could not be opened.)
rules.regional_note: One source is Taiwanese and notes that Westerners may hand over a card with one hand; for mainland business contacts both hands is the safe choice.

rules.rule: WeChat at work: (1) don't send a bare 在吗 ('are you there?') and wait; greet and state your request in the same message; (2) type rather than send voice messages, especially to superiors and clients, and if voice is really needed ask first (方便语音吗？); (3) for important messages, confirm receipt (收到) or ask the other person to confirm; (4) avoid sending work messages before 8:00 or after 22:00; (5) keep work group chats for work.
rules.why: A workplace survey reported by 中国新闻网 (2022) found 在吗 as a greeting widely disliked, and 'typing, not voice' among the etiquette points working people care about most; workplace articles (界面, 澎湃, 新浪) say strings of long voice messages burden the receiver and that voice messages are generally tolerated only from superiors to subordinates; WeChat etiquette for government offices (共产党员网, 2018) recommends confirming receipt of important messages and not sending work messages before 8:00 or after 22:00, and the result set also advises against off-topic chat in work groups. (Search-result summaries; which page made which point is partly inferred, and the pages could not be opened.)

scenes.title: Meetings: opening, running and closing
scenes.description: Opening and chairing a meeting, asking for and giving views, adding a point, agreeing and deciding, closing, and the small talk around a meeting with visitors. Built only from official HSK/BCT test material, the 2021 national grammar standard, 现代汉语词典 and CC-CEDICT (web search was unavailable this session); several common target phrases from the brief (我们开始吧, 我补充一点, 我有个问题, 今天就到这里) could not be verified and are listed in open_questions.

phrases.pinyin: Zuò hǎo ba, yào kāihuì le.
phrases.literal: sit well + suggestion-particle, about-to hold-meeting + particle
phrases.english: Please take your seats, the meeting is about to start.
phrases.usage: What the person in charge may say to get people seated: 好 after a verb means the action is properly done (坐好 'be seated, sit properly'), 要…了 means 'is about to'. It is an instruction, so a visitor or junior would not say it; to start a meeting yourself, say 我们开始吧 (work.meetings.lets-begin). This is the dictionary's own example (现代汉语词典, entry 好 ❼). A firmer variant from the same dictionary (entry 大家): 大家安静点儿，现在开会了 (Dàjiā ānjìng diǎnr, xiànzài kāihuì le) 'Everyone, a bit quieter please, the meeting is starting'.

rules.rule: Chinese has set politeness formulas (客套话) for ending a presentation of your own work by inviting correction or comments, e.g. 有不对的地方请大家指正 or 有不完备的地方，请多提意见.
rules.why: 现代汉语词典 defines 指正 ❷ as a 客套话 'used to ask people to criticise one's own work or views' and gives these examples. Leaving it out is not an error, but using it sounds modest and polished.

rules.rule: 辛苦了 / 大家辛苦了 ('thanks for your hard work') is said freely by the person in charge to staff, including in work group chats. When your manager writes it to you, reply with thanks plus a commitment (e.g. 谢谢领导，我会继续努力的) rather than 不辛苦. Towards seniors, a host greeting a visitor after a journey with 路上辛苦了 is standard; for your own boss, add specific thanks (谢谢您的帮助) rather than relying on a bare 辛苦了.
rules.why: A 2024 光明网 article (WebSearch summary) treats leaders' 辛苦了 in work chats as routine courtesy and recommends a 'thanks + commitment' reply; the official HSK 5 sample has a host greeting a senior professor with 路上辛苦了, and the HSK 4 sample has the reply 感谢您的支持和鼓励，我一定会继续努力. No source seen settles whether a bare 辛苦了 to one's own boss is fine, hence the cautious advice.

phrases.pinyin: Zhè piān gǎozi nín fèishén kànkan ba.
phrases.english: Could I trouble you to take a look at this draft?
phrases.usage: Asking a senior colleague to review your text. 费神 'spend effort' is used as a 客套话 when asking a favour (现代汉语词典, with this example), and 看看 softens the verb. It is formal and much rarer than 麻烦您: 费神 does not occur at all in the native-speaker dialogue corpora or the HSK/BCT papers checked, where 麻烦您/麻烦你 occurs about 2,100 times. For everyday requests use 麻烦您 (work.requests.please-resend). Other formulas with the same function in the same dictionary: 劳神 (劳神代为照顾一下) and 有劳 (这件事有劳您了 'thank you for taking this on').

phrases.hanzi: 我理解你的想法，但我有不同的看法。
phrases.pinyin: Wǒ lǐjiě nǐ de xiǎngfǎ, dàn wǒ yǒu bùtóng de kànfǎ.
phrases.literal: I understand your thinking, but I have different view
phrases.english: I understand your thinking, but I see it differently.
phrases.usage: Disagreeing politely: acknowledge first, then give your view, then back it up with a reason or example (the three steps taught in Chinese-learning guides). A more formal guide example: 我理解您的立场，但我觉得我们可以从另一个角度来看这个问题 'I understand your position, but I think we could look at this from another angle'.

Tones: CC-CEDICT gives 倒是 dàoshi and 价钱 jiàqian (neutral second syllables, used here); 现代汉语词典 writes 倒是 dàoshì and the 2025 HSK list writes 价钱 jiàqián.

phrases.english: We'll look into it.
phrases.usage: Literally 'study it (a bit)': a classic answer to a request. 现代汉语词典 uses it in its own example for 代名词: 他所说的“研究研究”不过是敷衍、推托的代名词 'what he calls "looking into it" is just a byword for stalling and declining'. So 我们研究研究 or 等研究后再答复你 ('we'll reply after we've looked into it', example under 答复) mean there is no decision yet, and may be a polite no. In meetings 研究 is also used literally (work.meetings.agenda).
phrases.speaker: them

sources.title: Article on how to reply when a leader writes 辛苦了 in a work group chat
sources.publisher: 光明网 (Guangming Online)

rules.rule: When you ask someone to do something, wrap the request in a politeness formula. Everyday choices: 麻烦您… (by far the most common), 拜托您…, and 辛苦 (辛苦您了 / 辛苦你了); the same words also thank someone afterwards (麻烦您啦！, 麻烦你们了, 辛苦你了). 现代汉语词典 also lists 费神…, 劳神… and 有劳您… as 客套话 for requests, but they are formal and rare today: recognise them rather than use them.
rules.why: 现代汉语词典 defines each of these as a formula used when asking for or thanking someone for a favour; official HSK dialogues use 麻烦您… and 辛苦你了 in exactly these functions. Frequency check by the reviewer: 麻烦您/麻烦你 occur about 2,100 times in the CrossWOZ and RiSAWOZ native-speaker dialogues and 拜托 14 times, while 费神, 劳神 and 有劳 do not occur at all there or in any HSK/BCT paper checked.

rules.rule: To disagree softly, concede first and use a light 'but': 只是 (lighter than 但是) or 不过. Concession patterns: X倒是X，就是… and A是A，不过…. Praise + 只是 + 能不能…? is the polite way to ask for a better price or terms.
rules.why: 现代汉语词典 defines 只是 (conjunction) as 但是（口气较轻） 'but, with a lighter tone' and 不过 (conjunction) as introducing a restriction or correction, 'the same as 只是'; 倒是 ❹ marks a concession. The official HSK 5 sample shows the negotiation pattern: 你们的产品确实挺好的，只是价钱上能不能再便宜些？

rules.rule: To disagree in a meeting: acknowledge the other view first (我理解你的想法 / 你的意思我完全理解), then give yours (但／不过我有不同的看法), then a reason or example. To turn something down, soften it (恐怕不行, 这个有点难) and offer an alternative with 您看可以吗？ Avoid a bare 不 or 不可能, which can sound harsh.
rules.why: Chinese-learning guides teach this acknowledge-view-reason structure and warn that 不可能 sounds harsh; native service dialogues (CrossWOZ, RiSAWOZ) show exactly the softened refusal followed by an alternative and 您看可以吗？

rules.rule: Refusing outright is felt to be awkward. Chinese reference examples describe people who are unwilling but find it 'not appropriate to refuse straight away' (不便马上回绝), who are 'too embarrassed to refuse' (不好意思拒绝), or who agree 'out of consideration for face' (碍于面子，只好答应了). Expect requests to be declined indirectly (a deferral, 'we'll look into it', 'let me think about it'), do not read a reluctant yes as enthusiasm, and soften your own refusals (这件事我实在帮不上忙; 这个问题让我考虑一下再答复你).
rules.why: Face (面子) is at stake: 现代汉语词典 illustrates 面子 with 你这话伤了他的面子 'what you said hurt his face' and 碍于面子，只好答应了. The examples come from a dictionary and the national grammar standard, not from a business-etiquette study, so treat the advice as a general tendency.

rules.why: Dictionary evidence for the meaning of these deferrals; how often they mean a definite no in today's business practice could not be verified with native commentary this session.

rules.rule: Use 您, not 你, when making requests to clients, superiors and older colleagues (麻烦您…, 谢谢您的帮助, 请您…). Official business-test texts use 您 to managers and clients throughout, and 你 between peers or downward.
rules.why: 现代汉语词典 defines 您 as 你 'with respect' (含敬意). Official BCT examples: 李总，请您在这份文件上签字。; 黄经理：您好！…有需要的话，请您和我们联系。

rules.rule: Say clock times as [day part] + [hour]点 + [minutes]分: 下午两点, 两点二十五（分）, 三点零五（分）; half past = 半 (五点半); quarter = 一刻 (五点一刻); 'to' = 差 (差两分八点 = 7:58). Two o'clock is 两点.
rules.why: Forms listed in the national grammar standard (level 1 time expressions) and 现代汉语词典 (刻); official business dialogues use 两点 for 2:00 and put the day part first (明天下午两点).

rules.rule: Three words for 'week': 星期 (standard), 周 (same meaning; common in schedules and writing: 周一, 下周), and 礼拜 (colloquial). Sunday is 星期日/星期天, 周日, or 礼拜天/礼拜日. 'Next week' = 下周 / 下星期 / 下礼拜.
rules.why: 现代汉语词典 defines 周 ❻ as 星期 and marks 礼拜 as 〈口〉 (colloquial); the official BCT timetable uses 周四/周五/周六; CC-CEDICT lists 下周 and 下星期 as 'next week'.
rules.regional_note: Whether 礼拜 is more common in southern Mandarin was not verified this session.

scenes.title: WeChat and email: openers, closers and conventions
scenes.description: Salutations, polite openers, acknowledging, sending documents, closing lines, sign-offs and the 贵/我 conventions of business correspondence. WeChat-specific etiquette (收到 vs 好的, emoji, reply times) could not be verified this session.

phrases.english: Dear Manager Huang,
phrases.usage: Opening of a business email in the current official BCT sample: surname + title, a full-width colon (：), then 您好！ (黄经理：/ 您好！…; another email: 吴秘书：/ 您好！…). For a company head use 总: 李总, 王总 (both appear in the same BCT sample). The brief's 'X总您好' was not seen as a written opener; the attested pattern puts the colon after the title.
phrases.speaker: me

phrases.english: Received. / Got it.
phrases.usage: 收到 'received / got it' is the standard short acknowledgement in work chats when your manager or a group posts a notice or an instruction; 好的 'OK' is also used, and both often come with thanks (收到，谢谢 / 好的，收到 are very common in native chat-style dialogue). Chinese career-advice articles agree that you should reply, and some advise adding what you will do or by when for a task instead of a bare 收到 (see work.writing.rule.wechat-acknowledge). 收到 is HSK 3 vocabulary (2025 list, shōudào); official texts also use it in full sentences: 来信收到了 (现代汉语词典), 我们已经收到贵方…的邮件 (BCT email).

phrases.english: Respectfully yours
phrases.usage: Traditional formal letter ending: 此致 'herewith (I extend)' introduces the salutation 敬礼 'salute'. Layout: after the body, start a new line indented two characters and write 此致; on the next line, flush left, write 敬礼 (often 敬礼！); then your name and the date. CC-CEDICT: 此致 '(used at the end of a letter to introduce a polite salutation)', 此致敬礼 'respectfully yours'; 现代汉语词典 敬礼 ❷ 敬辞，用于书信结尾. Learner guides call it the safest closing for very formal letters and emails (to bosses, clients, people you don't know well); some find it a bit dated for everyday email, where 祝好 or a wish such as 祝工作顺利！ is common. 此致 is level 7-9 vocabulary in the 2025 HSK list.

rules.rule: Layout of business letters and emails in the official samples: (1) salutation on its own line, flush left: surname + title, or 尊敬的 + addressee, followed by a full-width colon (黄经理： / 尊敬的领导： / 尊敬的用户：); (2) 您好！, on its own line or starting the first paragraph; (3) the body, paragraphs indented two characters in letters; (4) a closing wish or thanks (祝工作顺利！ / 谢谢！ / 最后，祝愿公司发展得越来越好！); for a very formal letter, write 此致 on a new line indented two characters and 敬礼 on the next line flush left; (5) the sender: company and/or person or department (今品公司 高小东; 天津腾飞公司总经理办公室), optionally phone and email (电话：…, Email：…); (6) the date (10月10日; 2023年10月20日).
rules.why: Observed consistently across official BCT sample letters, emails and notices from Hanban (c. 2012-13) and CLEC (2023-24); the 此致 / 敬礼 placement, which the samples do not use, follows Chinese letter-format guides.

rules.rule: When your manager or a work group posts a notice or an instruction, reply promptly: 收到 ('received / noted') or 好的 ('OK') is the standard short acknowledgement, often with thanks (收到，谢谢). For a task, add what you will do or by when instead of a bare 收到.
rules.why: Chinese workplace commentary (36氪, 界面新闻, a career article reposted on Tencent Cloud; WebSearch summaries) disagrees on 收到 versus 好的 but agrees that a reply is expected and that 收到 shows you have seen the message; some recommend '收到 + plan' for instructions. Native chat-style dialogue shows 收到，谢谢 and 好的，收到 as everyday acknowledgements. Expected reply times were not found in any source.

rules.rule: Avoid the WeChat 微笑 smiley (the default [微笑] face, similar to 🙂) with colleagues and clients: many younger Chinese read it as cold or sarcastic ('nothing more to say', like 呵呵), while many older people, including managers, use it as a sincere smile, so don't read too much into it when they send it. When in doubt, say it in words.
rules.why: Reported by CNA (2019: in mainland China young netizens send the smile after being offended, meaning 'nothing more to talk about') and 虎嗅 (2024: most middle-aged and older leaders still read it as a smile); a Shanghai labour dispute turned on whether a colleague's smiley was mockery (the court held it could not simply be read as mockery), which shows how ambiguous it is.

rules.rule: Some letter formulas are old-fashioned or literary: 现代汉语词典 says 敬启者 was formerly used to open letters (旧时用于书信的开端) and marks 见谅, 来书 and 感纫 as 〈书〉 (literary). The current official BCT samples (2023-24) instead open with name + title + 您好！ and close with a wish or 谢谢！.
rules.why: Helps a learner avoid stiff, antiquated openings; the modern alternative is what the official samples show.

terms.usage: Everyday word for father, to address him and to talk about him (CC-CEDICT '(coll.) father'; HSK 1). In HSK samples children address their fathers as 爸爸 or the short 爸 ('爸，您为什么要问我这么简单的问题？'). For your partner's father: normally from the wedding on (改口), earlier only if the parents invite it; before that he is 叔叔 or 伯父.
terms.regional_note: relationship.js lists many colloquial/regional alternatives (e.g. 老爸, 爹, 阿爸, 老汉) without regions — note that in standard Mandarin 老汉 means 'old man' (现代汉语词典); its Guangdong locale gives the Cantonese 老窦. Xinhua: 大大 is a dialect word for father ('方言。称父亲'); CC-CEDICT: '(dialect) dad / uncle'.
terms.group_title: Father's side: father, grandparents, uncles and aunts

terms.usage: Address and everyday reference (CC-CEDICT '(coll.) paternal grandfather; grandpa'; HSK 2). Formal/written equivalent: 祖父. Also a respectful title for any old man, usually with the surname (HSK 2025 syllabus: 张爷爷; Xinhua sense 3 '对男性尊长的称呼').
terms.regional_note: relationship.js's Guangdong locale gives the Cantonese 阿爷; its main list also has 阿公, 嗲嗲, 爹爹 and others (regions not stated). Careful with 爹爹: 现代汉语词典 marks it 〈方〉 with two senses, 'father' and 'grandfather', so listen to how your partner's family uses it. 阿公 and 公公 are dialect words (〈方〉) for grandfather (现代汉语词典, Xinhua).
terms.group_title: Father's side: father, grandparents, uncles and aunts

terms.usage: Everyday word for mother, to address her and to talk about her (CC-CEDICT 'mama; mommy; mother'; HSK 1). Children address her as 妈妈 or the short 妈 (HSK samples: '妈妈，谢谢您！', '妈，您的手机响了。'). For your partner's mother: normally from the wedding on (改口), earlier only if the parents invite it; before that she is 阿姨 or 伯母. 你妈 is fine inside a sentence (Tatoeba: '你和你妈用上海话聊天的时候…'), but as a bare exclamation it is a curse (CC-CEDICT), so 你妈妈 sounds gentler when you speak of your partner's mother.
terms.regional_note: 姆妈 is a dialect word for mum (CC-CEDICT '(dialect) mom; mother'; 现代汉语词典 〈方〉 ❶母亲); relationship.js lists further variants (阿妈, 老妈, 娘, 姆妈 …) without regions; its Guangdong locale gives the Cantonese 老母.
terms.group_title: Mother's side: mother, grandparents, uncles and aunts

terms.usage: Address and everyday reference (CC-CEDICT '(coll.) mother's father; maternal grandfather'; Xinhua: 外祖父 '俗称外公'). 外 marks the mother's side. In the new HSK 5 sample a four-year-old tells her grandfather '外公，我在幼儿园能自己穿衣服…' and he calls her 外孙女. HSK 2025 level 5, the same level as northern 姥爷.
terms.regional_note: The everyday word in the south. 现代汉语词典 labels 外公 〈方〉 and gives 姥爷 without a label; when a Shanghai primary-school textbook replaced 外婆 with 姥姥 in 2018, the change caused a public outcry (chinanews.com). relationship.js lists 外公 first by default and uses 姥爷 in its 北方 (northern) locale; Cantonese: 阿公. Its main list also has 外爷, 家公, 嘎公 and others (regions not stated). Xinhua: 公公 is also a dialect word (〈方〉) for maternal grandfather.

terms.usage: CC-CEDICT: 'older male cousin through a female relative'; 表 = 'family relationship via females'. Xinhua: 表哥 = 表兄, '姑母、舅父、姨母之子，年长于己者称表兄'. relationship.js names the branches 姑表 (via father's sister), 舅表 (via mother's brother) and 姨表 (via mother's sister). These cousins can be on either side of the family: 姑表 cousins on your father's side, 舅表 and 姨表 cousins on your mother's. address_form is an inference: no source here says whether cousins are called by the full term (堂哥, 表姐) or just 哥/姐; Xinhua's 姐姐/弟弟/妹妹 entries do cover older/younger relatives of the same generation in the clan.

terms.english: (north, colloquial) wife — usually 媳妇儿 xífur; read xífù, 媳妇 means daughter-in-law
terms.usage: HSK 2025: xífu (level 6). The two senses differ in pronunciation: CC-CEDICT xífu '(dialect) wife; (dialect) young married woman' vs xífù 'daughter-in-law; wife of a younger brother or relative of the younger generation'; 现代汉语词典 likewise has 媳妇 xífù (son's wife; wife of a younger relative: 侄媳妇, 孙媳妇) and 媳妇儿 xí·fur 〈方〉 (wife; young married woman). Xinhua: '方言。北方称妻子'. So in the north 我媳妇儿 is 'my wife'; as 'daughter-in-law' the standard word is 儿媳妇.
terms.regional_note: 'Wife' is the northern dialect sense (Xinhua: 方言。北方称妻子).

rules.rule: Each uncle and aunt has a specific term that says which side and which relative: on your father's side his older brothers are 伯伯/伯父, his younger brothers 叔叔, his sisters 姑姑 (older or younger alike); on your mother's side her brothers are all 舅舅 and her sisters 姨/姨妈.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 伯伯 'father's elder brother', 叔叔 'father's younger brother', 姑姑 'paternal aunt', 舅舅 'mother's brother', 姨妈 'mother's sister'. relationship.js keeps the same split: 'f,ob' 伯父/伯伯, 'f,lb' 叔叔, 'f,xs' 姑妈/姑姑, 'm,xb' 舅舅, 'm,xs' 姨妈.

rules.rule: Several relatives of the same kind are numbered by birth order (排行): 大 for the eldest (大伯, 大姑, 大舅, 大姨), then 二, 三, 四… (二叔, 三姨), and 小 for the youngest (小姑, 小姨). Some regions use other words for 'youngest', which relationship.js treats as equal to 小 (e.g. 幺, 细, 满, 尾).
rules.why: Xinhua 排行: '兄弟姐妹依长幼排列的次序'. CC-CEDICT: 大伯 'father's older brother (esp. his oldest brother)', 大姑 'father's oldest sister', 小姑 'father's youngest sister', 大姨 'mother's eldest sister', 小姨 'mother's youngest sister', 老幺 '(coll.) youngest child'. relationship.js numbers relatives 大 = 1, 二, 三 … and 小 = last, and rewrites the prefixes 尕, 幺, 细, 满, 碎, 晚, 末, 尾, 幼 to 小.
rules.regional_note: relationship.js does not say which 'youngest' prefix belongs to which region.

rules.rule: Most relatives have an everyday term, often doubled (爷爷, 伯伯, 叔叔, 姑姑), and a formal/written one (祖父, 叔父, 姑母); you call people by the everyday term. 伯父/伯母 are the exception that also serve as respectful titles.
rules.why: Xinhua: 外祖父 '母亲的父亲。俗称外公' (commonly called 外公), 外祖母 '…俗称外婆'. CC-CEDICT marks everyday forms as colloquial — 爷爷 '(coll.) paternal grandfather; grandpa', 姑妈 '(coll.)', 婶子 '(coll.)' — and calls 伯父 a 'term of respect' and 伯母 a 'polite form of address'. HSK 2025 puts 爷爷/奶奶 at level 2 but 祖父/祖母 at level 7-9.

rules.rule: 外 ('outside') marks relatives through a woman: 外公/外婆 (mother's parents), 外孙/外孙女 (daughter's children), 外甥/外甥女 (sister's children). The counterparts through a man have no 外: 爷爷/奶奶, 孙子/孙女, 侄子/侄女.

rules.rule: For the mother's parents there are two pairs: 外公/外婆 and 姥爷/姥姥. Both are taught (HSK 2025, level 5) and understood everywhere. 姥爷/姥姥 is the northern pair and the one the 现代汉语词典 treats as standard, labelling 外公/外婆 〈方〉; but 外公/外婆 is the everyday pair in the south — when a Shanghai textbook replaced 外婆 with 姥姥 in 2018, it caused a public outcry. For a family from south/central China expect 外公/外婆 (or a local word) — check with your partner.
rules.why: relationship.js main list 'm,f':['外公',…,'姥爷',…], 'm,m':['外婆',…,'姥姥',…]; 北方 locale 'm,f':['姥爷'], 'm,m':['姥姥']; readme example setMode('northern', {'m,f':['姥爷'], 'm,m':['姥姥'], …}). HSK 2025: 外公 wàigōng, 外婆 wàipó, 姥爷 lǎoye, 姥姥 lǎolao, all level 5.
rules.regional_note: North: 姥爷/姥姥; south: 外公/外婆; Cantonese: 阿公/阿婆 (relationship.js locales; 现代汉语词典 labels; 2018 Shanghai textbook controversy).

rules.rule: Cousins are 堂 or 表. 堂 cousins are your father's brothers' children (the paternal line, same clan); 表 cousins are the children of your father's sisters, your mother's brothers and your mother's sisters. Then add 哥/姐/弟/妹 by sex and by age relative to you: 堂哥, 表妹…
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 堂 'relationship between cousins etc on the paternal side of a family / of the same clan'; 表 'family relationship via females'; 堂哥 'older male patrilineal cousin'; 表哥 'older male cousin through a female relative'. Xinhua 表兄: '姑母、舅父、姨母之子，年长于己者称表兄'; 姑表 vs 姨表 name the two kinds of 表 link. relationship.js prefixes: 'f,xb' 堂, 'f,xs' 姑表, 'm,xb' 舅表, 'm,xs' 姨表.

rules.rule: In-law words depend on whose family it is: a wife's in-laws are 公公/婆婆 (together 公婆; his family is her 婆家); a husband's in-laws are 岳父/岳母, colloquially 丈人 (老丈人) and 丈母娘 (her parents' home is the 岳家; for her it is her 娘家). Face to face, after 改口, both say 爸/妈.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT: 公婆 'husband's parents; parents-in-law', 婆家 'husband's family (traditionally where the wife moves into)', 岳父 'wife's father', 岳母 'wife's mother', 丈人 'wife's father', 老丈人 '(coll.) father-in-law (wife's father)', 丈母娘 'wife's mother', 岳家 'wife's parents' home', 娘家 'wife's family (before marriage)'; Xinhua 娘家: '已婚女子称自己父母的家'. rules.rule: The -子 words for a spouse's siblings — 大伯子, 小叔子, 大姑子, 小姑子 (husband's) and 大舅子, 小舅子, 大姨子, 小姨子 (wife's) — are colloquial words for talking about them, not titles to call them by. rules.rule: Once you are married, call your partner's relatives what your partner calls them (随配偶称呼): the parents 爸/妈; the grandparents 爷爷/奶奶 or 外公/外婆; uncles and aunts 伯伯, 叔叔, 姑姑, 舅舅, 姨… and their spouses; your partner's older siblings 哥/姐 and their spouses 嫂子/姐夫; younger siblings by name, as your partner does. The in-law words (公公, 婆婆, 岳父, 大伯子, 小姨子…) are for talking about them.
rules.why: CC-CEDICT 改口: a bride 'starts to call her husband's parents 爸爸 and 妈妈'. A guest post on Speaking of China, written for Western women married to Chinese men, says that besides 公公/婆婆 'in many cases, people just use the same words as their husband use, which are 爸 or 妈', and that with the older generation 'just to follow your husband is fine'; ETtoday (2026-05-17) reports that following one's spouse in calling the in-laws 爸爸/媽媽 after marriage is still widespread. CC-CEDICT 小姨子: '(term not used to directly address her)'.
rules.regional_note: Another custom names some in-laws from your children's point of view (Xinhua 叔叔 ②: '丈夫的弟弟' — a wife calling her husband's younger brother 叔叔). Local habits differ: check with your partner.

items.title: Basic word order: subject + time + place + verb + object
items.rule: Statements are Subject + Verb + Object (我们学中文). Words that say when, where, how or with whom go BEFORE the verb: Subject + (Time) + (在/从 + Place) + Verb + (Object) — 他十点睡觉, 哥哥在北京学中文. A time word normally follows the subject, or opens the sentence when the time is stressed. Adverbs (不, 也, 都) and modal verbs also stand before the verb; with a modal the order is Subject + Time + Modal + 在/从-phrase + Verb. One everyday exception: with 住 'to live, to stay' the 在-phrase normally follows the verb (你住在哪儿？ 你住在什么地方？), and verbs of putting or sending do the same (放在桌子上, 送到车站; see grammar.ba). Questions keep statement order (see grammar.question-words).
items.details: Official grammar syllabus (GF 0025-2021, level 1): 动词谓语句 [一25] and 'adverbs, adjectives, time and place words as adverbials' [一28] — 他十点睡觉。我们下午去吧。她在网上买了两本书。哥哥从北京回来了。; 跟/和 + person before the verb [一17] — 他跟老师请假了。我没和姐姐一起去中国。; manner before the main verb [三56] — 我明天坐飞机去北京。 发展汉语 (初级上 第5课) gives the order 主语—动词—宾语 and says adverbials normally go before the verb; 第16课: 在 + place goes before the verb, '一般情况下，介词结构不能放在动词后边'. 成功之路 (起步篇1 第6课): time words go before the verb, or at the start of the sentence when the time is emphasised. 发展汉语 (初级上 第17课): time adverbials go before a modal verb, place and prepositional phrases after the modal and before the main verb. To learn later: verbs of placing put 在/到 + place AFTER the verb to say where something ends up (老师把书放在桌子上了, 我把朋友送到车站了; see grammar.ba). Level: 2025 HSK syllabus, HSK 1 (状语: 表示时间、处所的词语作状语).
items.common_mistake: Putting the place phrase (or the time) at the end as in English: *哥哥学中文在北京 → 哥哥在北京学中文; the time also goes before the verb: 他十点睡觉.

items.title: 是 links two nouns: A 是 B
items.rule: Noun/Pronoun A + 是 + Noun B = 'A is B' (identity, category, job, nationality): 他是我的老师, 这是他的书. 是 has the same form for every person and tense. Negative: 不是 (not 没是). Question: …是…吗？ or 是不是. 是 is not used to link a subject with an adjective (see grammar.hen-adjective).
items.details: Official syllabus [一36] '是'字句 (1) 表示等同或类属: 他是我的老师。这是他的书。; (3) 表示存在: 车站东边是一个学校。教学楼西边不是图书馆。 发展汉语 (初级上 第1课): the 是-sentence does not change for person or number (他是老师); negative 马克不是老师。 成功之路 (起步篇1 第1课): 是 states a judgement — what something equals or belongs to; the negative uses 不. Dates, ages and prices are often said without 是 (名词谓语句: 明天星期五, 这本中文书二十五块; see grammar.time). Level: 2025 HSK syllabus, HSK 1 ('是'字句1).
items.common_mistake: Using 是 before an adjective (*我是很忙; see grammar.hen-adjective) and negating 是 with 没 (*没是) instead of 不是.

items.title: Adjective predicates: subject + 很 + adjective (no 是)
items.rule: Subject + 很 / 非常 / 真 / 最 (or 太…了) + Adjective. The adjective is itself the predicate, so 是 is NOT used (*我是很好). In a plain positive statement a degree word, usually 很, is added; this 很 is unstressed and does not really mean 'very' — a bare adjective implies a contrast (这个苹果大，那个苹果小). Negative: 不 + Adjective (今天不冷). Questions: Adjective + 吗 (你忙吗？) or Adj.-不-Adj. (你忙不忙？).
items.details: Official syllabus [一30] 主谓句2：形容词谓语句 (房间很干净。这个学生最认真。), [一25] (今天不冷。这个菜很好吃。), [一09] 程度副词 非常、很、太、真、最. 1996 grammar syllabus (甲级, quoted in the reference CSV): '形容词谓语句，谓语中不用“是”：今天很热。' 成功之路 (起步篇1 第5课): no 是 before an adjective predicate; 很 is commonly added in the positive, is read lightly and does not express a marked degree; without 很 the sentence implies a comparison; the negative puts 不 before the adjective. 发展汉语 (初级上 第10课): S + Adj. with no 是 — '不能说“我是很好”'; in a contrast (这个苹果大，那个苹果小) no degree adverb is needed. Different pattern: 是…的 describing a characteristic (花是白的。衣服是干净的。 [一36]). Level: 2025 HSK syllabus, HSK 1 (主谓句2：形容词谓语句).
items.common_mistake: Inserting 是 as if it were English 'to be': *我是很好 / *房间是很干净 → 我很好 / 房间很干净.

examples.english: The room is clean.

items.title: 有 / 没有 (to have, there is) and 在 (to be located)
items.rule: Possession: Subject + 有 + Object ('have'): 我有一个弟弟. Existence: Place + 有 + (number + measure word) + Noun ('there is / there are'): 房间里有两张桌子. The negative of 有 is always 没有 (or 没), never *不有, and after 没有 the object normally has no number: 房间里没有桌子. Location of a particular person or thing: Person/Thing + 在 + Place ('is at / in'): 书在桌子上; negative 不在: 爸爸跟妈妈都不在家. An ordinary noun becomes a place with a position word: 桌子上, 书包里, 房间里.
items.details: Official syllabus [一37] '有'字句1: (1) 表示领有 我有很多书。他没有哥哥。一个星期有七天。 (2) 表示存在 房间里有两张桌子。房间里没有桌子。; [一01] 方位名词 (桌子上 书包里边 …; 书在桌子上。手机在书包里。房间里没有人。); [一19] 爸爸跟妈妈都不在家。 成功之路 (起步篇1 第2课): 有 means possession; the negative uses 没, not 不, and the negated object takes no number. 国际汉语教学通用课程大纲 (quoted in the reference CSV): 主语+有/没有+宾语 (我有一个弟弟) and 方位短语+有+名词 (桌子上有两本书). Level: 2025 HSK syllabus, HSK 1 ('有'字句1 表示领有; 存现句1 处所+有+数量短语+名词; 介词 在).
items.common_mistake: *不有 instead of 没有 (*他不有哥哥 → 他没有哥哥), and keeping a number after 没有 when you simply mean 'there is none': say 房间里没有桌子, without 两张. (没有 + number means something else, 'not even / less than': 来了没有三天就走了 'left before three days were up'.)

examples.english: I have a younger brother.

items.title: Negation: 不 vs 没(有), and 别
items.rule: 不 + Verb/Adjective = 'not / don't / won't': for adjectives (今天不热), habits and likes (我不喜欢看电视), what someone does not do or will not do (他不去医院), and before 是, 在 and modal verbs (不是, 不在, 不会). 没(有) + Verb = 'didn't / haven't': the action did not take place (他昨天没上课, 我今天没有吃早饭); in this negative the completion 了 is dropped (他买了两个面包 → 他没买面包). 有 is negated only with 没: 没有. Experience keeps 过: 没去过. 别 + Verb = 'don't!' (你别进来).
items.details: Official syllabus [一14] 否定副词 别、不、没、没有 (你别进来。今天不热。他昨天没上课。我今天没有吃早饭。), [一29] (他不去医院。), [一32] (我不喜欢看电视。), [一02] (我不会说中文。), [一41] (他买了两个面包。／他没买面包。), [二32] (我去过一次中国。／我没去过中国。). 1996 grammar syllabus 甲116 (via the reference CSV): the negative of a completed action is 没(有) before the verb, normally without 了. 成功之路 (起步篇1 第2课): 有 takes 没, not 不. CC-CEDICT: 没 '(negative prefix for verbs) have not; not'; 不 'no; not so; not'. Tone: 不 is pronounced bú before a fourth tone (不去 bú qù, 不热 bú rè) — see 'spoken'. Level: 2025 HSK syllabus, HSK 1 (否定副词 不、没（有）、不要); 别 HSK 2.
items.common_mistake: Using 不 for something that did not happen (他昨天没上课, not 不上课, when you mean he didn't go), saying *不有, and keeping 了 after 没 (*他没买了面包 → 他没买面包).

examples.english: It isn't hot today.

items.title: Yes/no questions: 吗 and the affirmative-negative (A-not-A) form
items.rule: (1) Statement + 吗？ makes a yes/no question without changing the word order: 他是老师吗？ 那儿现在热吗？ (2) A-not-A: say the verb or adjective, then 不 + the same word: 你喝不喝牛奶？ 今天冷不冷？; a two-syllable word can be repeated whole (干净不干净？), but in everyday speech usually only its first syllable is repeated: 喜不喜欢？ 高不高兴？ For completed actions: …了没有？ (你吃早饭了没有？) or Verb + 没 + Verb (你吃没吃早饭？). The middle 不 is read lightly. Answer by repeating the verb or adjective, positive or negative (我买书 / 我不买). An A-not-A question does not take 吗.
items.details: Official syllabus [一45] 用'吗'提问 (他是老师吗？这包子好吃吗？), [一33] 疑问句: 是非问句 (他是老师吗？那儿现在热吗？) and 正反问句 (你喝不喝牛奶？你吃没吃早饭？你吃早饭了没有？今天冷不冷？这个房间干净不干净？), [一48] (这本书贵不贵？电影好看不好看？他回家了没有？). 发展汉语 (初级上 第10课): Adj.+吗 / Adj.+不+Adj., '其中“不”要轻读'; 第11课: S+V+不+V+(O)? is answered 我买书 / 我不买（书）; 第17课: with a modal verb the A-not-A form is modal + 不 + modal + verb. Level: 2025 HSK syllabus, HSK 1 (是非问句, 正反问句).
items.common_mistake: Answering every question with 是 / 不是. Reply with the question's own verb or adjective: 你喝不喝牛奶？ — 喝。/ 不喝。 Also, don't add 吗 to an A-not-A question: *这是不是书吗？ → 这是不是书？ or 这是书吗？

items.title: Question words: 什么, 谁, 哪儿/哪里, 哪, 几, 多少, 怎么, 为什么, 什么时候, 怎么样
items.rule: Put the question word where the answer will stand; the rest keeps statement order, and the question word itself makes the sentence a question (the syllabus examples have no 吗). 什么 what (你买什么？); 谁 who (谁是老师？); 哪儿 / 哪里 where — same meaning; 哪儿 is the northern, colloquial form and 哪里 the usual one in the south and in writing (你们去哪儿？ 车站在哪里？); 哪 + measure word which (你喜欢哪个电影？ 她是哪国人？); 几 + measure word how many — for small numbers (about 1–10), measure word required (现在几点？ 你家有几口人？); 多少 how many / how much — any number, measure word optional (你的电话号码是多少？ 多少钱？); 怎么 + verb how (你怎么去医院？); 为什么 why (你为什么不去上课？); 什么时候 when (你们什么时候见面？); 怎么样 how is…? / how about…? (明天天气怎么样？).
items.details: Official syllabus [一04] 疑问代词 多、多少、几、哪、哪儿、哪里、哪些、什么、谁、怎么 and [一46] (你家有几口人？她是哪国人？我们在哪儿见面？这个字怎么读？), [二05] 多久、为什么、怎么样、怎样, [二76] 什么时候、什么样、为什么、怎么样、怎样. 发展汉语 (初级上 第2课): in 你是哪国人？ / 你叫什么名字？ the question word keeps the word order of the statement. 成功之路 (起步篇1 第4课): 几 asks about numbers from 1 to 10 and normally needs a measure word; 多少 asks about any number and the measure word is optional (你们班有多少学生？). 发展汉语 (初级上 第8课): 几 cannot go straight before a noun (你家有几口人？); 第12课: phone numbers are read digit by digit and 1 is usually read yāo. HSK考试大纲 一级 (via CSV): 你这几本书多少钱？ 1996 grammar syllabus 甲103 (via CSV): 请问，去车站怎么走？ 'Excuse me, how do I get to the station?'. 多少 here is duōshao (CC-CEDICT and HSK: 'how much? how many?'). Level: 2025 HSK syllabus — 多、多少、几、哪、哪儿、哪里、哪些、什么、谁、怎么、怎么样 HSK 1; 为什么 HSK 2. Regional note: 哪儿 / 这儿 / 那儿 are erhua forms, marked 〈口〉 (colloquial) in 现代汉语词典 and typical of northern speech; southern Mandarin generally has no erhua, so in south/central China, and in writing, expect 哪里 / 这里 / 那里. Both sets are standard and understood everywhere.
items.common_mistake: Moving the question word to the front as in English (*什么你买？ → 你买什么？) and putting 几 straight before a noun or using it for large numbers (*几学生 → 几个学生, or 多少学生); and adding 吗 to a question-word question (*你是谁吗？ → 你是谁？). 吗 goes with a question word only inside a 'do you know…?' question: 你知道这是什么吗？

items.title: 呢: 'And you?', 'Where is…?' and follow-up questions
items.rule: (1) After a statement, Noun/Pronoun + 呢？ asks the same thing about someone or something else: 我去医院，你呢？ ('…and you?'). (2) Noun + 呢？ also asks where something is: 书在桌子上，笔呢？ ('…and where's the pen?'), 你的词典呢？ (3) 呢 can end a question that already contains a question word (他是哪国人呢？). (4) At the end of a statement 呢 marks an action in progress (我在看书呢) — see grammar.zai-progressive. A plain yes/no question uses 吗 (grammar.ma-questions).
items.details: Official syllabus [二77] 用'呢'构成的省略式疑问句'代词/名词+呢？' (我去医院，你呢？书在桌子上，笔呢？), [一22] 语气助词 呢 (他是哪国人呢？我在看书呢。), [二50] dialogue 甲：你的词典呢？乙：不好意思，我没拿来。, [二26] (她后天过生日，我们给她送什么礼物呢？). 1996 grammar syllabus 甲108 (via CSV): 我们下星期去旅行，你呢？/阿里，你的车票呢？/要是他不同意呢？ CC-CEDICT 呢: '(sentence-final particle) used in questions to link back to prior discourse or context ("what about...?", "and...?"); …indicating that a state or situation still holds'. Level: 2025 HSK syllabus — 呢1–呢3 HSK 1, 呢4 HSK 2.
items.common_mistake: Using 呢 as if it were 吗: 呢 asks 'and X?' or 'where is X?' or follows up a question word; to turn a statement into a yes/no question use 吗.

examples.english: I'm going to the hospital — and you?

items.title: Measure words: number / 这 / 那 / 哪 / 几 + measure word + noun
items.rule: A number or 几 must have a measure word (classifier) before the noun: Number + MW + Noun (两个人, 三本书, 两杯牛奶). 这/那/哪 normally take one too: 这/那/哪 + (number +) MW + Noun (那个书包, 这本书, 哪个电影), although 这/那 directly before a noun also occurs in speech (the syllabus has 这包子好吃吗？). 'Two' on its own before a measure word is 两, not 二 (两个, 两本); inside a bigger number the tens and units digits stay 二 (十二个, 二十二个). Common ones: 个 (people and nouns with no special MW), 本 (books), 杯 (a cup/glass of), 口 (people in a family), 家 (shops, firms), 件 (clothes, matters), 张 (flat things: tables, tickets, sheets), 位 (people, polite), 块 (pieces; in speech also yuan: 二十五块). 这个 / 那个 / 哪个 can stand alone: 'this one, that one, which one'.
items.details: Official syllabus [一08] 名量词 杯、本、个、家、间、口、块、页 (两杯牛奶 三本书 四个学生 五家商店 六间房子 三口人 七块面包), [一07] (两个人 两本书), [一23] 数量短语 (一个 两杯 三本 四包 五块), [二10] 层、封、件、条、位 (一件衣服 一位老师), [三09] 把、张、双… (一张桌子), [一43] 钱数表示法 (九块三（毛）; 一百五十（块）). 发展汉语 (初级上 第9课, via CSV): 两 can go before every measure word (两个、两本、两张), 二 only before a few weight/length units (二斤); in speech the currency units 元、角、分 are called 块、毛、分; 第8课: 几 cannot go straight before a noun. CC-CEDICT: 个 'classifier used before a noun that has no specific classifier'; 本 'classifier for books, periodicals, files etc'; 张 'classifier for flat objects, sheet'; 位 'classifier for people (honorific)'; 件 'classifier for events, things, clothes etc'; 口 'classifier for things with mouths (people, …)'; 家 'classifier for families or businesses'; 块 '(coll.) classifier for money and currency units'. In speech 个 is often unstressed; the citation tone is gè. Level: 2025 HSK syllabus — HSK 1: 本、个、家、口、块、件、只、元, 杯; HSK 2: 条、位、间、名, 包; HSK 3: 把、双、张、种…
items.common_mistake: Leaving out the measure word (*三书 → 三本书; *几学生 → 几个学生) and using 二 before a measure word (*二个 → 两个; but 十二个).

examples.pinyin: Nǐ hǎo, wǒ yào liǎng gè běnzi.
